- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) or mixed, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–2% to account for mean reversion or short-term rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > true outcome by >5%), model frequently overcorrects; cap forecast at 1–2% above true value for next period.
- If true outcome shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive days rising), model often lags; adjust forecast to align with 2nd or 3rd day’s true trend.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model tends to misalign with sentiment direction; align forecast with sentiment’s most recent dominant polarity.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates early in the forecast window; apply a 1–3% downward bias for days 1–5, then revert to normal trend.
- If sentiment is negative and price is rising, model may misread sentiment; reduce forecast by 1–3% to avoid overconfidence in upside.
- If sentiment is positive and price is falling, model may overreact; reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid “sentiment-driven overcorrection.”
